subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

repairs.reason: register backfill (founder ruling 2026-08-02; testing.md C3 / ARV-D-011..013, ARV-D-026)

edits.note: 'one behaviour they will practise in school' is the commitment

periods.textbook_anchor: Green School — Walk around the school and create its map including main building, playground, garden, water tanks and other key features (p. 56)

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to name their favourite spots in school and briefly share what makes their school feel like a happy, safe place. The class hears a few responses and the teacher introduces the idea of a school that is also a 'green school' — one that manages waste, saves water, uses electricity wisely, and is full of plants.

Students read the opening story of Aasha and Mohit in Textbook p. 56 and then step outside in an orderly group with paper and pencil for a guided walk around the school campus. They observe the main building, playground, garden, water tanks, pathways, and gate.

Back in the classroom, students draw a map of their school on blank paper, placing the key features they observed. They label each feature clearly. The teacher circulates, prompting students to check whether their map shows entry and exit points and the pathways that connect areas.

A few students share their maps briefly with the class. The teacher draws out responses to: 'What did you notice while walking that you had never paid attention to before?' Students then write two or three sentences in their notebooks responding to Textbook p. 57 — what they really like about their school.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent a familiar physical environment as a labelled map, identifying key features and their spatial relationships.
periods.section_context: School campus walk, map-making activity including main building, playground, garden, water tanks, gate, pathways; written reflection on what students like about school.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether the map they drew matches their classmate's map — open question: 'Did everyone show the same things? Why might maps look different?' Prompt groups to compare and notice differences in what each person chose to include.

periods.activity_title: School Explorer Teams: Observe and Report
periods.textbook_anchor: Green School — Walk around your school and create its map. Include the main building, playground, garden, water tanks and other key features (p. 56)
materials: observation recording sheets (blank paper or notebooks)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the five School Explorer Team roles: Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, and Traffic Trackers. The class discusses what each team would look for — leaking taps, lights left on, litter, plants and trees, and traffic behaviour near the gate. Each team of five or six students receives a simple observation prompt written on the board for their area.

Teams move through their assigned areas of the school with notebooks, recording what they observe using words or quick sketches. Water Watchers check taps; Electricity Savers check classrooms and corridors; Waste Warriors look for litter and bins; Green Guardians count and sketch plants; Traffic Trackers observe the gate area from a safe vantage. Teacher accompanies each group briefly to keep inquiry focused.

Teams return to class and organise their notes. Each team writes three key findings on the board or a shared space. The teacher connects findings to the 'green school' concept, drawing out the idea that small observations reveal how a school is actually functioning. The teacher gently introduces how people in many communities — using traditional practices like cleaning with cow dung and mud — have long kept spaces cool and clean, asking students if they have seen or heard of similar practices at home or in their neighbourhood.
Quick oral debrief: each team answers one reflection question — 'What surprised you most about what you found?' Students note one action their team would recommend in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured field observation, record findings systematically, and share them in a group discussion.
periods.section_context: School Explorer Teams (Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers); observation of leaking taps, wasted electricity, litter, plants, traffic near school gate; team findings discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask teams: 'Did different members of your group notice different things, even in the same area? What does that tell us about observation?' This surfaces the idea that structured roles and shared inquiry produce richer findings than individual looking.

periods.textbook_anchor: Waste Management — Make small paper chits with names or drawings of items and sort them into boxes labelled green (wet waste), blue (dry waste), and items for recycler (p. 61)
materials: small blank paper chits (30–40 per group)
three boxes or containers per group labelled with colour and category name
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing green bin (wet waste) and blue bin (dry waste) colour coding

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the three-category waste system: wet waste (green bin), dry waste (blue bin), and items for the recycler. Students respond to Textbook p. 59 — naming which colour bin is for dry and wet waste — and write their answers in notebooks. The teacher briefly mentions that in many communities, people who collect old newspapers, glass, and metals have long practised this kind of material recovery, often known by different names in different regions.

In groups of four or five, students prepare 30–40 paper chits following Textbook p. 61, writing or drawing the names of items found at school or home. They add at least five items they think of themselves. Each group sets up three labelled containers.

Groups carry out the sorting activity from Textbook p. 61 — one student picks a chit at a time and places it in the chosen container while the group watches and silently decides whether they agree. Once all chits are placed, the group opens each container and discusses whether every item was sorted correctly, moving any they disagree with.
Whole-class discussion on Textbook p. 62: what happens if waste is not separated? Students note one surprising mis-sorting moment from their group's activity in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into waste categories using defined criteria and justify their sorting decisions.
periods.section_context: Wet waste (green bin) and dry waste (blue bin) colour coding; items for recycler; paper chit sorting activity; consequences of not separating waste.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask each group: 'Was there any item where your group disagreed about which container it belonged in? What made it tricky?' This surfaces borderline cases (e.g. a wet paper napkin, a broken pen) and deepens understanding of the criteria.

periods.activity_title: Black and White Tiles — Heat Absorption Experiment
periods.textbook_anchor: Let Us be Cool! — Take two tiles or stones, paint one black and the other white, keep them under the Sun, then touch each and feel the difference in temperature (p. 62)
materials: two identical tiles or flat stones

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a class discussion: 'Have you ever noticed that some rooms in school feel much hotter than others on a sunny day? What might cause that?' Students share observations. The teacher connects responses to the idea that dark surfaces absorb more heat and light surfaces reflect it, and mentions that in many villages, floors are traditionally cleaned with cow dung and mud — a practice that also helps keep the house cool.

In pairs or small groups, students paint one tile black and one white following Textbook p. 62, then place both tiles under direct sunlight in a safe area of the school compound. While the tiles heat up, students draw a simple prediction table in their notebooks: which tile will feel hotter, and why they think so.

After an unhurried wait in the sun, students return to their tiles and carefully touch each one, recording their observation — which felt cooler, which felt hotter, and whether it matched their prediction. Students then respond to Textbook p. 63: if you painted the school roof white, what would happen?

Class discussion on Textbook p. 63: if the area around school is getting warmer, what actions could be taken to keep it cool? Students name at least three practical actions — trees, white roofs, ventilation — and write them in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple comparison test, record observations, and connect results to a real-world application.
periods.section_context: Black and white painted tiles or stones; heat absorption and reflection comparison; white roofs and trees as cooling strategies; ventilated windows; traditional mud and cow dung floor practice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Before students touch the tiles, ask: 'Which one do you predict will be hotter — and what is your reason?' After the experiment, ask: 'Did the result surprise anyone? Did anyone's prediction turn out to be wrong?' This keeps inquiry honest and models scientific temper.

periods.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Find a dripping tap or poke a small hole in a water bottle, collect dripping water in a glass, measure the time to fill it, and calculate how many glasses would fill in a day (p. 64)
materials: pin or needle to make a small hole

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds students of what the Water Watchers team noticed during the school exploration — leaking taps. The class is asked: 'How much water do you think one dripping tap wastes in a whole day?' Students make a quick guess in their notebooks. Teacher introduces clay pots (matkas) as a traditional way to keep water cool without electricity, connecting to the idea that managing water wisely has long been part of Indian household practice.

In small groups, students set up the experiment from Textbook p. 64 — a small hole in a filled water bottle simulates a dripping tap. They collect the drip into a glass and time how long it takes to fill. They record the time, then calculate: how many times would that glass fill in one hour? In one day? Each group records its measurements in a simple table.

Groups share their numbers with the class — the teacher writes results on the board and the class compares. Discussion: even small differences in drip rate lead to very different daily totals. Students discuss Textbook p. 64: what are some easy things schools can do to prevent water wastage?

Students discuss and then write one or two sentences responding to Textbook p. 64: how could rainwater be collected and used at school or at home? The teacher briefly mentions the Jal Shakti Abhiyan campaign as a civic effort aligned with what the class has just measured.

periods.implied_lo: Students can collect and use measurement data to estimate the scale of a resource-use problem and propose practical conservation responses.
periods.section_context: Dripping tap or small hole in water bottle; glass collection and timing; daily water wastage calculation; water conservation actions at school; rainwater collection; clay pot (matka) as traditional cooling vessel; Jal Shakti Abhiyan.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'If every tap in our school dripped at this rate, how much water would be lost across the whole school in a day?' This scaling question connects individual measurement to collective impact and builds the case for conservation action.

periods.activity_title: Tree Shade Temperature Experiment and Campus Greenery Record
periods.textbook_anchor: Greenery Around Us — Take two glasses of water, measure temperature, keep one under a tree and the other under the Sun, measure again after one hour, and record readings (p. 66)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Where would you choose to sit during a hot afternoon in school — under a tree or on an open bench? Why?' Students share responses and name specific trees they know on the campus. Students then complete the observation record from Textbook p. 65 — naming trees on the campus or near school, and noting which birds and insects they have seen near plants and trees.

Groups set up the experiment from Textbook p. 66 — two glasses of water, temperature measured and recorded, one placed under a tree and one in direct sunlight. While waiting for results, students discuss with the teacher the role trees play: shade, clean air, food and habitat for birds and insects, and cooling the environment. The teacher introduces the Ladakh ice stupas — tall ice towers built by students that melt slowly in summer to water school gardens — as an example of a traditional engineering response to water scarcity.

Groups return to measure and record the temperature of both glasses following Textbook p. 66. They write their readings in a table and answer: what do these readings tell us? The class compares results across groups and the teacher helps them articulate the conclusion in their own words.

Class discusses the idea of planting trees that attract birds and butterflies and planning a butterfly garden for the school campus, as suggested in Textbook p. 66. Students write one sentence about which tree or plant they would recommend planting and why.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use temperature measurements to compare the cooling effect of natural shade and record observations that support an evidence-based conclusion.
periods.section_context: Two glasses of water — under tree and under sun; temperature measurement with thermometer; campus trees named; birds and insects near trees; butterfly garden planning; Ladakh ice stupas as traditional water-management example.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After results are in, ask: 'By how many degrees did the temperatures differ? Is that difference big enough to matter for people and animals living in this campus all day?' This connects data to lived experience and builds ecological reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Designing a School Gate Safety Signboard
periods.textbook_anchor: Traffic Signs — Find out and write at least three traffic rules (p. 67)
materials: chart paper or A4 paper (one sheet per group)
periods.visual_aids: Board notes listing three to four common traffic signs for reference

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a brief discussion of Thomas's concern about road accidents near school from the chapter's story context. Students share what they have noticed at the school gate during arrival or dismissal — who is present, what vehicles do, whether pedestrians are safe. The class then responds to Textbook p. 67 — each student writes at least three traffic rules in their notebook and shares one with the class.

Students respond to Textbook p. 67 — writing two or three observations about what happens at their school gate. Teacher collects a few responses aloud and uses them to frame the design challenge: what kind of safety signboard would address what they actually observed?

In teams of four or five, students design a safety signboard for the school gate on chart or A4 paper, using words, drawings, or symbols as they choose. Each team decides what message their board will carry and for whom — drivers, parents on bikes, pedestrians, or students themselves. Teams are encouraged to make the message clear enough that someone who cannot read can still understand it through a symbol or image.

Teams display their signboards on desks or the board. A quick gallery walk allows each team to observe others' designs. The class discusses one question from Textbook p. 68: besides signboards, what else could students do to improve traffic near school? Two or three responses are noted on the board.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of civic safety rules to design a clear visual communication for a public audience.
periods.section_context: Three traffic rules written by students; observations at school gate; safety signboard design using words, drawings, or symbols; actions to improve traffic near school.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask each team: 'Who is the audience for your signboard — drivers, pedestrians, or students? Does your design speak clearly to that audience?' This sharpens student awareness of purpose-driven communication in public spaces.

periods.activity_title: Fire Drill Role-Play and Safety Planning
periods.textbook_anchor: Fire Safety — Write what you should do if there is a fire or if you smell smoke (p. 69)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing the six-step fire drill procedure

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Have you ever heard a fire alarm or done a fire drill before? What did you do?' Students share briefly. The teacher explains that staying calm and knowing exactly what to do is more important than speed, and introduces the six-step fire drill procedure written on the board: move calmly to exits, crawl under smoke, avoid hiding places, help others safely, reach the assembly point, and alert staff.

Students complete Textbook p. 68 — writing where the fire extinguisher is kept in their school and where the assembly point is. If students do not know, the teacher supplies the information. Students also write their response to Textbook p. 69 — what they should do if they smell smoke — using the six steps as a guide.

In groups, students role-play a calm, orderly fire drill inside the classroom — practising moving toward the door without running, pretending to crawl under imaginary smoke below desk height, reminding a partner not to hide under a desk, and saying the name of the assembly point aloud as they exit. The teacher narrates the scenario and pauses to ask the class whether each group's actions matched the six steps.

Whole-class reflection: what is the hardest step to remember when you are frightened? Students write one sentence about what they will do differently now that they have practised. Teacher reinforces that fire preparedness is a shared responsibility — every student who knows the steps helps keep everyone safer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and apply a structured emergency procedure through role-play, and explain the reasoning behind each step.
periods.section_context: Fire extinguisher location in school; assembly point; six-step fire drill procedure (calm exit, crawl under smoke, no hiding, help others, assembly point, alert staff); what to do when smelling smoke.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After the role-play, ask: 'Why is crawling under smoke a better choice than running upright through a smoky corridor?' This question checks conceptual understanding of the step, not just recall of the sequence.

periods.activity_title: Scenario Discussion — What Would You Do?
periods.textbook_anchor: What We do Matters! — In small groups, discuss the situations given and share ideas with the class (p. 70)

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the discussion: 'We have been thinking about how to make our school greener and safer. Now we think about something equally important — how we treat each other and the spaces we share.' The teacher introduces the idea that behaviour in everyday moments shapes whether a place feels welcoming or uncomfortable for everyone.

The class divides into five groups. Each group is assigned one scenario from Textbook p. 70: (1) pushing and skipping the queue at the water tap; (2) a student scribbling on a bench while another watches silently; (3) a wrapper thrown in the playground copied by a younger student; (4) a student teasing and making fun of another; (5) a group making noise in a public park disturbing others. Each group discusses: what would they do if they saw this happening, and what steps could prevent it? One student from each group prepares to share.

Each group's representative shares their scenario and the group's response with the class. The teacher facilitates brief whole-class reactions after each one, drawing out the idea from Textbook p. 70 that respect and kindness are shown through everyday actions, not just big gestures.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: one behaviour they will practise in school and why it matters. Teacher affirms that awareness of how our actions affect others is itself a form of learning.

periods.implied_lo: Students can analyse everyday social scenarios, evaluate the impact of behaviour on shared spaces, and propose constructive responses.
periods.section_context: Five behaviour scenarios: queue-skipping at tap, bench scribbling with silent bystander, littering copied by younger student, teasing a classmate, noise in public park; discussion of what to do and how to prevent incidents.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For scenario 2 (silent bystander), ask the class: 'Is doing nothing the same as allowing something to happen? Why or why not?' This question deepens thinking beyond obvious right-and-wrong and surfaces the concept of bystander responsibility.

periods.activity_title: Happiness Tree and Letter to Teacher
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Create a happiness tree on chart paper; each student adds a leaf with one small action that makes school a happier place (p. 71)
materials: one large sheet of chart paper
smaller paper cut into leaf shapes (one per student)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with: 'We have observed our school, sorted waste, measured water, investigated heat, mapped trees, designed signs, practised fire safety, and talked about how we treat each other. What is one thing that has stayed with you?' Students share briefly. The teacher introduces the two creative tasks for this unit: the Happiness Tree and the letter to the teacher from Textbook p. 71.

The class works together to create the Happiness Tree from Textbook p. 71 — a large tree is drawn on chart paper and pinned or taped to the board or wall. Each student receives a paper leaf, writes one small action on it that makes school a happier place (greeting someone, turning off lights, sharing space, picking up litter, watering a plant), and adds it to the tree. The teacher reads a few leaves aloud and connects them to themes the class explored: water, waste, greenery, kindness.

Students write a letter to their teacher on the theme 'My School — My Happy Place' following Textbook p. 71. The letter should mention what they appreciate about their school and one thing they personally commit to doing. Students who finish early begin a second task from Textbook p. 71 — writing about one action from school they would extend to their home, neighbourhood, or community.

Two or three students read their letters aloud, or the teacher reads selections with permission. The class reflects: 'Is there anything on the Happiness Tree that we could actually do together as a class starting this week?' The teacher affirms that thinking about how our actions shape shared spaces — whether a school, a neighbourhood, or a public park — is the heart of what this chapter has been about.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of community responsibility through a creative personal letter and a collaborative visual display, connecting individual actions to shared wellbeing.
periods.section_context: Happiness Tree on chart paper with individual action leaves; letter to teacher on 'My School — My Happy Place'; extending school-based values of happiness, safety, and care to home, neighbourhood, and community.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If someone who had never visited your school read your letter, what would they understand about what kind of place it is and the people who care for it?' This question lifts the letter from description to reflection on shared values.

assessment_items.question_text: A student walks around the school to draw a map. She marks the main building, playground, and water tanks. She also adds the school gate and the pathways between areas. What does including pathways on a school map tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Pathways are drawn only to make the map look complete and colourful.

options.label: B
options.text: Pathways show how different parts of the school are connected and how people move through the space.

options.label: C
options.text: Pathways show where the tallest building in the school is located.

options.label: D
options.text: Pathways tell us how many students study in the school.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests the student's understanding that a map represents spatial relationships, not just individual features in isolation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent a familiar physical environment as a labelled map, identifying key features and their spatial relationships.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused a map's spatial function with a data-recording function — a map of the campus does not carry enrolment information.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused a pathway (route between areas) with a landmark or building — indicating a misunderstanding of what different map features represent.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student treats map-making as decoration rather than as a tool for representing real spatial relationships — suggesting they have not grasped the purpose of a functional map.

assessment_items.question_text: A School Explorer team assigned as Water Watchers walks around the school. They find two leaking taps near the toilets and one broken drain cover. Write two things the team should record about the leaking taps and explain why recording these details is useful.
expected_elements: Two specific details to record — for example: location of each tap, how fast the water is dripping, how long the tap has been leaking, or whether a container is catching the drip.
An explanation of why recording details is useful — for example: so the information can be reported accurately to a teacher or school authority, or so the problem can be tracked and fixed.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two reasonable observation details. The key quality marker is whether the student links recording to a purpose — reporting, fixing, or tracking — rather than just listing observations without a reason.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured field observation, record findings systematically, and share them in a group discussion.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Two specific, observable details about the leaking taps (location, rate of drip, duration, or whether water is being collected).
A stated reason for why recording these details is useful — connecting observation to action such as reporting to a teacher, scheduling a repair, or monitoring whether the problem worsens.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is sorting waste using three containers: a green box for wet waste, a blue box for dry waste, and a third box for items to give to recyclers. She picks up a used glass bottle. In which box should she place it, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Any box, because colour coding of bins does not apply to glass.

options.label: B
options.text: Blue box, because glass is dry waste that does not rot.

options.label: C
options.text: Green box, because glass was used to hold a liquid.

options.label: D
options.text: Recycler box, because all glass must be sent to a recycler immediately.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests whether students understand that the wet/dry distinction is about whether the material decomposes, not about its previous contents or liquid association.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into waste categories using defined criteria and justify their sorting decisions.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing the material's nature (glass = dry) with its previous use (held liquid) — a common category confusion in waste classification.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows recyclers handle glass but has missed that the recycler box is for items specifically set aside for them, not all recyclable material placed there directly — conflating two steps in the system.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student believes colour-coded bin rules have exceptions based on material type — indicating the bin system criteria have not been internalised as universal within the school waste framework.

assessment_items.question_text: Two students conduct an experiment. They paint one stone black and one stone white, place both in sunlight for the same amount of time, and then touch each stone. The black stone feels much hotter. Name one place in a school building where this finding could be applied to keep the space cooler, and explain how.
expected_elements: A specific location in the school — for example: the roof, the outer walls, a classroom floor, or a sunlit corridor.
An explanation of how the finding applies — stating that using a white or light colour at that location would reflect sunlight and reduce heat absorbed, keeping the space cooler.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any reasonable school location. The quality marker is whether the student explains the mechanism (reflection reduces heat absorption) rather than simply saying 'paint it white'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple comparison test, record observations, and connect results to a real-world application.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A named location in the school building where the colour-heat principle can be applied (roof, wall, floor, corridor).
An explanation that links the experiment result to the application — lighter colour reflects sunlight, reducing the amount of heat absorbed by that surface, making the connected space cooler.

assessment_items.question_text: A group of students pokes a small hole in a filled water bottle to simulate a dripping tap. They time how long it takes for the drip to fill one glass. It takes 12 minutes to fill one glass. How many glasses of water would drip in one day (24 hours)? Show your working. What does this tell us about a leaking tap in school?
expected_elements: Correct calculation: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 glasses per hour; 5 × 24 = 120 glasses per day.
A statement connecting the number to the significance of the waste — for example: one small dripping tap wastes a large amount of water every day, making it important to fix leaks quickly.
assessment_items.annotation: Full marks for correct calculation (120 glasses) with working shown AND a meaningful statement about waste. Partial credit if calculation is correct but no connection is made, or if working is absent but the answer is correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect and use measurement data to estimate the scale of a resource-use problem and propose practical conservation responses.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Step-by-step calculation showing glasses per hour (60 ÷ 12 = 5) and then glasses per day (5 × 24 = 120).
An interpretive statement explaining that even a slow drip accumulates into significant wastage over a full day, reinforcing the importance of fixing leaks as a water conservation action.

assessment_items.question_text: Students place one glass of water under a tree and one glass of water in direct sunlight. After an unhurried wait, the glass in sunlight measures 38°C and the glass under the tree measures 28°C. What can students correctly conclude from these readings?

options.label: A
options.text: The difference in temperature shows that the two glasses contained different amounts of water.

options.label: B
options.text: The sunlight glass was hotter because it was a different type of glass from the one placed under the tree.

options.label: C
options.text: The tree provided shade that reduced heat absorption, keeping the water under it cooler than water in direct sunlight.

options.label: D
options.text: The water under the tree became cooler because tree roots absorbed the heat from the glass.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item checks whether students attribute the temperature difference to shade blocking solar radiation rather than to an unrelated variable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use temperature measurements to compare the cooling effect of natural shade and record observations that support an evidence-based conclusion.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student understands that the tree caused the cooling but has invented an incorrect mechanism (root absorption) — showing partial conceptual understanding that needs refinement toward shade and radiation blocking.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student introduces an uncontrolled variable (amount of water) that was not varied in the experiment — indicating a misunderstanding of how a controlled comparison works.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student attributes the result to a material difference between the glasses — showing they have not connected the experimental variable (sunlight vs. shade) to the outcome.

assessment_items.task: Design a safety signboard for the school gate. Your signboard should carry a clear message for one specific audience — drivers, pedestrians, or students arriving at school. Use words, a drawing, or symbols (or a mix) to make your message clear even to someone who may not be able to read.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: Who is your audience? What is the one most important message for them at the school gate? How can you show your message clearly using an image or symbol alongside words?
format_of_output: A drawn or written signboard on paper
One sentence below the signboard naming the intended audience and explaining the message
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any signboard that (a) targets a named audience, (b) carries a safety-related message connected to the school gate, and (c) uses at least one visual element. Regional variations in traffic rules or signage conventions are acceptable — there is no single correct design.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of civic safety rules to design a clear visual communication for a public audience.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate civic safety knowledge into a purposeful communication product aimed at a real audience — moving from knowing a rule to communicating it effectively.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts three design decisions: identifying the audience, selecting the most important message, and choosing a visual form. A strong response will show evidence of all three; a weaker one will produce a generic sign with no specific audience or a list of rules rather than a focused message.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: single clear message, named audience, image or symbol that communicates independently of text. Weak: multiple messages that compete, no visual element, or a sign that copies an existing road sign without adaptation to the school gate context.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write their message in large clear words with a border or colour scheme that signals its purpose. Students who prefer working in their home language may write text in that language as long as a symbol or image carries the meaning across language boundaries.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The C&E mode of this unit and the C-code's emphasis on behavioural norms in public spaces both call for a product that demonstrates purposeful communication, not just recall of traffic rules.

assessment_items.task: Your teacher has asked your class to practise a fire drill. You are asked to explain the correct steps to a younger student who has never done a drill before. Write or draw the steps in the right order so the younger student can follow them easily.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What is the very first thing you do when you smell smoke or hear the fire alarm? What should you do if there is smoke in the corridor? Where should you NOT go? Where should you go at the end?
format_of_output: Written steps in numbered order OR a drawn sequence of images
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that include at least four of the six steps in a logical order, communicated clearly enough for a younger student to follow. The key marker is logical sequencing, not verbatim recall of the textbook procedure.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and apply a structured emergency procedure through role-play, and explain the reasoning behind each step.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student has internalised the fire drill procedure well enough to explain it to someone else — a transfer task that goes beyond simple recall to ordered communication.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides sequencing through four checkpoint questions (first action, smoke in corridor, where not to go, final destination). A strong response uses these anchors to build a coherent sequence; a weaker one lists tips without clear ordering.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four or more steps in logical order, at least one step explained rather than just named (e.g. 'crawl under smoke because smoke rises'), child-friendly language. Weak: fewer than four steps, steps out of order, or a list that mixes fire safety facts with unrelated safety rules.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw each step as a simple sketch with a label. Students who are more comfortable with a different Indian language may write step labels in that language. Drawn sequences count fully if the order and actions are clear.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The R&A mode of this unit requires demonstrated procedural knowledge — the task tests whether students can represent and order a safety procedure, not just recall that a fire drill exists.

assessment_items.question_text:
Read the situation below and answer the question.

Rahim is standing in the queue at the school water tap. Two students push ahead of him, skipping the line. Another student nearby sees this happen but says nothing and looks away.

What would you do if you were Rahim? What would you do if you were the student who saw it happen but said nothing? Explain why the bystander's silence also matters in this situation.
look_for: A response for Rahim's position that goes beyond simply reporting to a teacher — ideally suggesting a calm, respectful way to address the queue-skipping directly.
A response for the silent bystander that recognises that doing nothing allows the behaviour to continue — acknowledging bystander responsibility.
An explanation of why the bystander's silence matters — connecting it to how norms are upheld or eroded in shared spaces, and the idea that choosing not to act is itself a choice.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit requires all three elements: Rahim's constructive response, the bystander's rethought response, and an explanation of why silence matters. Partial credit where two elements are present. Responses that reduce the bystander dimension to 'the bystander should tell the teacher' without explaining the principle of shared responsibility are adequate but not strong.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse everyday social scenarios, evaluate the impact of behaviour on shared spaces, and propose constructive responses.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Rahim's response: a constructive action that addresses the situation without aggression — such as calmly saying 'the queue starts here', asking a nearby adult for support, or assertively but politely pointing out the shared norm.

Bystander's rethought response: the student moves from silence to some form of acknowledgement or gentle intervention — recognising that their presence gives them a small role in whether the behaviour is normalised.

Explanation of bystander silence: the student articulates that silence can signal acceptance, that others watching may interpret it as approval, and that shared spaces depend on multiple people upholding norms — not just the person directly affected.

assessment_items.task: Write a letter to your teacher with the title 'My School — My Happy Place'. In your letter, mention: one thing you genuinely appreciate about your school, one action from school that you would like to carry to your home or neighbourhood, and why that action would make your community a better place.
assessment_items.scaffold: Begin by thinking about something in your school that makes you feel safe, happy, or proud. Then think about one action — something small that anyone can do — that could make your home or neighbourhood feel the same way. In your letter, explain why this action matters.
format_of_output: A letter addressed to the teacher
Three parts addressed: appreciation, extended action, and reason
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine appreciation and any transferable action connected to the chapter's themes (water, waste, greenery, kindness, safety, traffic). There is no single correct answer. Regional variations in community practices are acceptable and should be encouraged.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of community responsibility through a creative personal letter and a collaborative visual display, connecting individual actions to shared wellbeing.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from describing a school as a place they know to analysing its role as a community institution — and whether they can connect values practised in school to broader civic responsibility.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the letter into three moves: appreciation (what the school does well), transfer (a portable action), and reasoning (why it matters beyond school). A strong response makes all three moves with specificity; a weaker one stays at the appreciation stage without transfer.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific, personal appreciation; a named action tied to a chapter theme; reasoning that explains community benefit rather than just personal preference. Weak: generic praise ('my school is very nice'), a vague action ('be good'), or no reasoning offered for the transfer.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find letter writing difficult may structure their response as three numbered points addressed to their teacher. Students may write in their home language if they choose; the quality markers apply regardless of language.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The C&E mode of this unit calls for an expressive, personal format. The letter form — addressed to a real person — encourages genuine reflection rather than generic response, and connects the individual to the institution being studied.
